title: The lord white as jasmine
hook: a queen's question goes unanswered in a hall of men, and a poet leaves a palace to sing to Shiva in her own words
carry: in bhakti, anyone can speak to god in their own words

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bilva tree, and a hunter who kept Shiva's holy night without knowing it. Today, another ridge.
screen: `THE RANGES AHEAD.` · `A NIGHT KEPT WITHOUT KNOWING.`

segments.voice: This year, in the dice game, Draupadi was dragged into a hall full of men and asked them a question. Had her husband lost himself before he staked her? If he had, was she his to lose? Bhishma answered that the way of dharma was too subtle for him to decide. Young Vikarna spoke up for her and was shouted down. Draupadi's voice reaches us inside a vast story told about her. But some women in this tradition left their own words behind, and one of them walked out of a palace to do it.
screen: `DRAUPADI'S QUESTION.` → `THE ELDERS CAN'T SETTLE IT.` → `A WOMAN, IN HER OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Akka Mahadevi lived in Karnataka in the twelfth century. The story told about her says a king wanted her, and she wanted only Shiva. She left the palace and, the story says, walked out into the world covered only by her own long hair, looking for her lord. She found her way to a circle of Shiva's devotees, poets like Basavanna and Allama Prabhu, who sang short free poems called vachanas, sayings, in Kannada, the language people spoke at home. Akka's vachanas speak to one beloved, her name for Shiva: Chennamallikarjuna, the lord white as jasmine. Some readers hear them as blunt and tender at once: a woman telling God, plainly, that she will have no other. That's the heart of bhakti, the path of loving devotion, and one of Hinduism's great turns. God can be loved directly, as your own, and spoken to in your own language, by anyone: a queen or a weaver, a man or a woman. It's why Hindu devotion lives in Tamil and Hindi, Kannada and Gujarati, not only in Sanskrit, and why grandmothers sing to God in the words they grew up with. Far to the north, Lal Ded, also called Lalla, did the same in Kashmiri. In one saying attributed to her, in paraphrase, she wandered far, searching, and found what she was looking for at home, inside. Year four sets these voices beside the women of the epics, not as a special topic, but as part of the main road.
screen: `AKKA LEAVES THE PALACE.` · `VACHANAS, IN KANNADA.` · `THE LORD WHITE AS JASMINE.` · `BHAKTI: GOD, IN YOUR OWN WORDS.` · then, large: `PART OF THE MAIN ROAD.`

segments.voice: Speak to God, or to whatever you hold highest, in the language you think in at home, not the one you'd use to impress anyone. One or two plain sentences, the way Akka spoke to her lord white as jasmine. If you don't pray, say them to the day ahead. Then sit for a few breaths and let the words settle, without fixing them.
Vachana. A saying: the short free poems Akka Mahadevi sang to Shiva in Kannada, her own language, the way bhakti speaks to God.
Your line: in bhakti, anyone can speak to God in their own words. Akka did, in Kannada. Tomorrow, one more ridge. Rest well.

howItsDone: Akka Mahadevi's vachanas are sung and recited in Karnataka and Lal Ded's sayings are quoted in Kashmir; across India, Hindus pray and sing bhajans to God in their own languages, as the bhakti saints did.
